title: Divided votes: which matters and which districts
question: Which kinds of land-use matter, and which districts, draw divided votes at the Board and at the commissions?
finding: At the full Board 81 of 1,618 land-use roll calls were divided (5.0%), most often on appeal of a conditional-use decision (13.0% of 131) and zoning map change or planning law for a named site (10.6% of 198). At the Planning Commission 169 of 897 decisions with a recorded vote were divided (18.8%), most often on new housing, 1 to 9 homes, or an in-law unit (35.7% of 42); by district of the address the share runs from 6.8% (District 7, 44) to 24.5% (District 2, 102).
how: Board: full-Board roll calls, one per vote, grouped by the kind of file and by the district printed in the title. Commissions: every action in the 2019-2022 minutes that approved, changed or disapproved an item and lists ayes; “divided” means at least one no is printed. The kind of proposal is read from the item’s description with the planning-applications screen’s rules; the district is that of the parcel or address under the 2012 district lines in force at the time. Groups with fewer than 20 votes are left out.
limits: The table shows divided votes varying more by kind of project than by place, and districts differ in how many of each kind they see. The Board’s titles print a district mainly for appeals and liquor licences. The minutes print a “(District N)” that is not always a supervisor district - 35 rows print 12 to 15 - so the district here is placed from the parcel instead; that looks like a quirk of the source, not of the decisions. A difference between areas, or between groups of cases, is not proof of bias. Areas differ in what is proposed, in zoning, lot sizes, building ages and land prices, and in who chooses to apply, object or appeal at all.
